title: Your share of your own lane
allegory: A feature's dimensionality is its share of its own lane: of all the traffic that runs along the direction it points in, what fraction is its own, so a feature alone in its lane scores 1 and one sharing it with an oncoming partner scores 1/2.
map: the unit direction Ŵᵢ that feature i is stored along
your own car in your lane
‖Wᵢ‖²: the feature's own squared length along its direction
other cars drifting into your lane
(Ŵᵢ·Wⱼ)²: each other feature's squared overlap with that direction
Dᵢ = ‖Wᵢ‖² / Σⱼ (Ŵᵢ·Wⱼ)², with j running over every feature, i included
an oncoming car in the very same lane
an antipodal partner: each of the pair gets exactly 1/2

chapters.name: Five into two
chapters.note: pretty shapes ... but how much room did each one get?

cap.1: A toy model squeezes five features into two dimensions, and their arrows form pretty shapes. How do you say, in one number, how much room each feature got?
cap.2: In the superposition toy model, W maps features into a small hidden space. You can plot the columns as arrows, but comparing arrangements by eye does not scale. You want a number per feature.
cap.3: Toy Models of Superposition (Elhage et al., 2022): W is (d_hidden, n_features). Dimensionality gives each column a scalar share of a dimension, making the geometry quantitative.

props.label: feature 3: a lane of its own = 1

cap.1: Each feature travels a lane, and its dimensionality is its share of that lane's traffic. Alone: 1. Two walking it in opposite directions: half each.
cap.2: Dimensionality asks: of all the squared overlap along feature i's direction, how much is feature i's own? No overlap from others gives 1; others leaning in shrink it.
cap.3: Dᵢ is feature i's own squared norm over the total squared projection of every feature onto its unit direction: its share of the energy along Ŵᵢ.

parts.note: how far each leans into my lane

cap.1: On top: your own size. Underneath: everyone's lean into your lane, you included. If nobody else leans in, top equals bottom and you get a full 1.
cap.2: Top: the feature's squared length. Bottom: the sum over all features, itself included, of squared overlap with its direction. Orthogonal to all others gives 1; an unused feature gives 0.
cap.3: Dᵢ = ‖Wᵢ‖² / Σⱼ (Ŵᵢ·Wⱼ)², equal to 1 iff Wᵢ is orthogonal to every other column. For a tight frame of n unit vectors in m dims, every Dᵢ = m/n.

chapters.name: Shapes into fractions
chapters.title: each feature's dimensionality in common shapes

cap.1: Each shape hands every feature a neat share: alone 1, an opposite pair 1/2, a triangle 2/3, a pentagon 2/5. The geometry turns into numbers.
cap.2: Opposite pair: 1/2 each. Triangle in 2D: 2/3. Pentagon in 2D: 2/5. Tetrahedron in 3D: 3/4. Features settle into these shapes, so their dimensionalities bunch at these fractions.
cap.3: Tight frames give D = m/n: digon 1/2, triangle 2/3, pentagon 2/5, tetrahedron 3/4, square antiprism 3/8. As sparsity varies, features jump between these values rather than sliding.

chapters.name: Long is not alone

left.title: norm ‖Wᵢ‖
lines: a long arrow can share its lane

right.title: dimensionality Dᵢ
lines: how much room it has alone

chapters.verdict: Length says it is there; dimensionality says whether it is alone.

cap.1: A long arrow means a feature is stored strongly, not that it has room to itself. Two long arrows pointing opposite ways still split one lane in half.
cap.2: Norm says a feature is represented; dimensionality says whether it is sharing. When you code it: normalise only Wᵢ, keep each Wⱼ raw, and include j = i in the sum.
cap.3: Norm measures representation strength; Dᵢ measures interference-free capacity. Implementation: Ŵᵢ unit-normalised, Wⱼ unnormalised, denominator includes the j = i term.

cap.1: Models seem to cram in more features than they have room for. Dimensionality measures the cramming, one feature at a time.
cap.2: In [1.5.4] you compute it for the toy model and watch features jump between fractions as sparsity changes. The same crowding is why sparse autoencoders exist.
cap.3: Per-feature interference separates a clean handle you can read or steer from a shared direction that will drag other features along when you push on it.

coda.title: Three features in two dimensions: share out the lanes

readouts.label: total (never more than 2, the number of dimensions)

caption.1: It starts as a triangle: 0.67 each, adding to 2. Set feature 3's length to 0 and feature 2's overlap to 0: two private lanes. Now try an overlap of −1.
caption.2: Sliders set cosines with feature 1 (feature 3 sits in the lower half-plane). Curves show each D as feature 2's overlap sweeps. The total never passes 2, the number of dimensions.
caption.3: W1 = (1, 0), W2 at cosine c12, W3 = L at cosine c13 (lower half). c23 = c12·c13 − √(1−c12²)√(1−c13²). ΣDᵢ ≤ m, with equality for tight frames such as the triangle.

where_else: Sparse autoencoders: an overcomplete dictionary of directions, the same crowding seen from the other side
Tight frames in signal processing: n directions sharing m dimensions evenly, m/n each
Packing problems like the Thomson problem: spread points on a sphere so overlaps stay small

hamming.what: A per-feature number for what fraction of a dimension a feature has to itself: 1 for its own lane, 1/2 when it shares one with an opposite partner.
hamming.when: When you study superposition in the toy model ([1.5.4]) and want to turn its geometric arrangements into numbers you can plot.
hamming.why: It makes superposition measurable feature by feature, which is what reveals sparsity pushing features into sharp, discrete sharing arrangements.

object.title: The share rack
object.subtitle: One bar per feature, as tall as its share of a dimension; swap the arrangement and watch the slices resize.

knobs.label: arrangement: 0 own lanes, 1 two opposite pairs, 2 triangle, 3 pentagon, 4 tetrahedron

cap.1: Two features in two dimensions, at right angles. Each gets a whole dimension: two full bars.
cap.2: Orthogonal columns: D = 1 each, total 2, the whole space used with no interference.
cap.3: Bar height = 1.5·Dᵢ. Orthonormal features: each Dᵢ = 1 and ΣDᵢ = m = 2.

cap.1: Four features as two opposite pairs, a plus sign. Each shares its lane with its opposite: half a dimension each.
cap.2: ±e1 and ±e2: each feature sees its partner's full length in its lane, so D = 1/2. Four halves still make 2.
cap.3: Antipodal pairs: D = 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2; the pairs are mutually orthogonal, so ΣDᵢ = 2.

cap.1: Three features fanned out in a flat plane: two-thirds each. Three bars that still add up to two.
cap.2: Triangle in 2D: each neighbour leans in with cos² 120° = 1/4, so D = 1/(1 + 1/4 + 1/4) = 2/3.
cap.3: Unit tight frame of 3 vectors in R²: D = m/n = 2/3, and ΣDᵢ = 2.

cap.1: Five in the plane, a pentagon: two-fifths each. More features means thinner slices, but the same total of two.
cap.2: Pentagon in 2D: D = 2/5 each. Sparse data makes this crowding worth it, because features rarely fire together.
cap.3: Five-vector tight frame in R²: D = 2/5. Interference cost scales with co-occurrence, which sparsity suppresses.

cap.1: Four features in three dimensions, a tetrahedron: three-quarters each, adding up to three.
cap.2: Tetrahedron in 3D: pairwise cosine −1/3, so D = 1/(1 + 3·1/9) = 3/4 each, total 3.
cap.3: Regular simplex in R³: D = 3/4 = m/n. Such fractions are where features' dimensionality tends to settle.

predict.q: Two features point in exactly opposite directions and nothing else overlaps them. What is each one's dimensionality?
predict.why: Each sees the other's full length in its own lane, so each gets half: 1/(1 + 1).

predict.q: A feature has a long arrow but shares its direction with others. Its dimensionality is...

options.t: Less than 1: length does not buy a private lane

predict.why: Dimensionality measures sharing, not strength. Overlap from others shrinks it however long the arrow is.

predict.q: Five features share a 2D space as a pentagon. What do their dimensionalities add up to?
predict.why: Each gets 2/5, and five of them fill the two dimensions exactly.

object.where: Any budget of directions shared by more things than it has room for: tight frames, SAE dictionaries.
